The unity we prize is frequently not unity at all. It is conflict-avoidance wearing the robes of maturity.

## The first ministry partnership ended in a fight

The most fruitful missionary partnership in the New Testament dissolved over a personnel dispute, and Luke records it without flinching.

> And some days after Paul said unto Barnabas, Let us go again and visit our brethren in every city where we have preached the word of the Lord, and see how they do. And Barnabas determined to take with them John, whose surname was Mark. But Paul thought not good to take him with them, who departed from them from Pamphylia, and went not with them to the work. And the contention was so sharp between them, that they departed asunder one from the other: and Barnabas took Mark, and sailed unto Cyprus. (Acts 15:36-41)

Barnabas — the *son of encouragement*, who vouched for Saul when the whole Jerusalem church was sure the persecutor was running a con — wanted to give his young cousin a second chance. Paul, who had felt the sting of John Mark abandoning the work at Pamphylia, said no. Not maybe. No. The Greek Luke chooses is *paroxysmos* — a sharp provocation, the word from which we get *paroxysm*. This was not a difference of opinion. This was a fight. Two men beaten and stoned and left for dead for the same gospel could not agree on whether one young man deserved another chance.

The Holy Spirit did not prevent it. Luke does not editorialize, does not assign blame, does not tell us which apostle was right. And both, it turns out, were partly right. Paul was right that the work was costly and a deserter is a liability. Barnabas was right that a deserter is also a person, and people can be restored. The gospel needed both convictions. It just could not fit them in the same boat that season.

## What the fight was not

The text never says they hated each other. It never says one of them sinned. It never says the kingdom shrank. There were now two missionary journeys where there had been one. Cyprus got Barnabas and Mark. Asia Minor got Paul and Silas. The disagreement did not contract the mission. It multiplied it. They divided the labor. They did not divide the church. No faction formed. No camp gathered in the parking lot afterward to decide who was spiritual and who was not. Two men reached the end of their agreement and remained brothers on opposite shores.

I have watched leadership teams take a disagreement one-tenth the size of this one and turn it into a fifteen-year cold war. The difference was never the size of the disagreement. The difference was always contempt. The moment I decide the brother across the table is not merely wrong but *bad* — not mistaken but malicious, not stubborn but spiritually deficient — the disagreement stops being about the question and starts being about him. And a team that has learned contempt cannot lead anything, because it has lost the one thing leadership runs on, which is trust.

## Fighting for the truth, or needing to win

This is the line I most often cross, and I have crossed it from a position of authority, which is the worst place to cross it from.

There is a kind of contending the truth requires. Paul contended. He withstood Peter to his face at Antioch. A leader who will not fight for the truth is not gentle. He is negligent, and his people will pay for his comfort. The objection comes quickly: *Are you asking leaders to go soft, to call every conviction divisive and every backbone pride?* No. That is the cheap reading, and it produces cowards who baptize their cowardice as humility. Steel in a leader is not a defect.

But underneath the fight for the truth there often runs a second river, and the two look nearly identical from the bank. One is the need for the truth to prevail. The other is the need for *me* to prevail. One can lose the vote and sleep fine, because the truth does not depend on my winning it. The other cannot lose anything without losing himself, because somewhere the truth and the ego fused.

You can tell them apart by one tell. When the man fighting for truth is proven wrong, he is relieved — the truth was served, and it cost him only his pride, which he did not need. When the man fighting to win is proven wrong, he is humiliated, and goes looking for a way to be technically right. The first can be corrected by a junior elder on a Tuesday. The second cannot be corrected by God.

Not every strong conviction is courage. Not every hill is the gospel's hill.

I have died on hills I chose because losing them would have embarrassed me, and told the room I was contending for the faith. I was contending for my standing. The faith was fine. It needed me to tell the truth and then submit to the body, and those are not the same act, and the second is the harder one, and I have skipped it more times than I will put in print.

## The reconciliation Paul never advertised

We love the fight because it is dramatic. We almost never preach the part that comes after. Years later, near the end, Paul is in a Roman prison writing his last surviving letter, and he asks for someone.

> Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee: for he is profitable to me for the ministry. (2 Timothy 4:11)

Take Mark. The same Mark. The deserter from Pamphylia, the cause of the sharpest fight in Paul's recorded ministry, the young man Paul refused to carry — and now, at the end of everything, the man Paul wants in the room. *Profitable to me for the ministry.* Barnabas had been right about the boy. Paul lived long enough to say so, not in a sermon or an apology tour but in a working request buried in a personal letter — which is exactly how reconciled men talk when the wound has actually closed.

The same Mark who left, by most accounts, wrote the Gospel that bears his name. The deserter Paul would not carry became the evangelist the church could not do without. Barnabas had seen it. Paul, eventually, saw it too. And it took years.

This is the formation a leadership team is for. Not the absence of the fight. The redemption of it.

## How you disagree in private is how you will lead in public

A congregation can always tell. Not the content of your conflicts — those stay behind closed doors. But the *spirit* of them seeps through every wall you build. A team that handles dissent with contempt will pastor with contempt, will preach at its enemies, will turn the pulpit into a settling of scores the people in the pews can feel but cannot name. A team that can disagree sharply and stay tender produces a church that holds the truth and holds each other at the same time. The people are formed by what they cannot see as much as by what they can. We keep asking how to build a church that disagrees without dividing, and we are answering it every month in the elder meeting, and the church is taking the exam home.

So the meeting where you lost the vote and wanted to make him pay for it — that was not a detour from the ministry. That was the ministry. The question was never whether the leaders of God's church would disagree. They will, sharply, as the two best of them once did over a young man who deserved a second chance. The question is whether, like Paul, you will live long enough and stay soft enough to one day send for the very person you could not carry, and call him profitable.

And if that question makes you uneasy about the last fight you won — good. That unease is the Spirit, still working in the room nobody can see.
reflect: Think of the last decision your team reached without disagreement. Was it unity, or was it the silence of people who decided naming the problem would cost too much?

When you were last proven wrong in a leadership conflict, were you relieved that the truth was served, or humiliated that you had lost? What does your honest answer reveal about which river you were fighting in?
Is there a "John Mark" you refused to carry — a person you wrote off in a past conflict — whom you have never gone back to call profitable? What would it cost you to send for them now?

chapters.title: Raising Your Replacement
chapters.summary: The leader who makes himself indispensable has failed at the one thing leadership is for — and finishing well means handing the towel to the next set of hands.
chapters.body:
The leader who cannot be replaced has failed.

Not slowed the work. Not made himself valuable. Failed — at the one thing leadership was ever for. We have spent eleven chapters on the towel and the basin, on power laid down, on the foot you would rather not wash. This last one asks the question that exposes whether any of it took root. When you are gone, does it stand — or does it fall, because you built it to need you?

Most of us have built it to need us. We did not mean to. It happened the way idolatry usually happens — slowly, and disguised as devotion.

## The Bottleneck With a Halo

Indispensability feels like faithfulness. That is what makes it so hard to see.

The pastor who answers every call, sits in every meeting, signs off on every decision — he does not look like a man with a problem. He looks like a man who cares. The congregation tells him they do not know what they would do without him, and he hears it as a compliment instead of a verdict. He has become the thing every healthy body learns to route around. He has become the bottleneck. And because the work is holy and the motive felt like love, no one names it for what it is.

A bottleneck with a halo is still a bottleneck.

The test is brutal and simple. Take the leader out and watch. If the ministry contracts, if the decisions stall, if the people stand around waiting for a voice that is no longer there — then what was built was not a body. It was an extension of one man's reach, and it dies when the reach ends. Eugene Peterson spent a career warning pastors off exactly this — the ego that disguises itself as availability, the machine that runs on the leader's importance and calls the dependence ministry. One is making disciples. The other is making a following.

I have built the following. I have stood in a room that ran because I was in it and mistaken the dependence for fruit. That is not humility. It is the confession of a man who learned late what the work was for.

## Reproduction Over Retention

The instinct of the insecure leader is to retain. Hold the relationships, the knowledge, the keys. Keep the people close enough that they cannot function without you, and call it shepherding.

The instinct of the servant is to reproduce. Give it away. Put the keys in younger hands and watch them turn the lock while you still have the strength to catch what they drop. Hear Paul, near the end, writing to a young man he is about to leave behind:

> "And the things that you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit these to faithful men who will be able to teach others also." (2 Timothy 2:2)

There are four generations in one sentence. Paul, who was taught. Timothy, whom Paul taught. The faithful men, whom Timothy must teach. And the others, whom those men will teach when Timothy is gone and Paul is long dead. Paul is in a cell, the sword is coming, and his concern is not his legacy or his platform or whether the churches remember his name. His concern is the chain — that the thing entrusted to him keeps moving past him, through hands he will never shake, to people he will never meet.

That is not retention. That is reproduction. Paul measured his ministry not by how many followed him but by how many he could send out from under his own shadow.

The faithful men is the load-bearing phrase. Not the gifted men, the natural communicators, the ones who fill a room. Faithful — the steady, the teachable, the ones still standing in twenty years when the charismatic ones have burned out or sold out or walked away. The leader obsessed with retention recruits the dazzling. The leader committed to reproduction invests in the faithful, because he is not building a crowd. He is building a chain for after him.

## Finishing Well Is Handing It On

We have made finishing well into a private achievement. The leader who keeps his marriage, his integrity, his name clean to the end — we are right to honor it. But there is a kind of finishing the New Testament cares about more, and it has nothing to do with your own preservation. You finish well when the thing outlives you because you trained it to outlive you.

Consider what Jesus did with three years. Twelve men were not ready, were going to fail in the first hours of pressure — and he handed them the whole thing anyway, and then he left. He left the kingdom in the hands of fishermen who had just abandoned him. That was not recklessness. That was the plan. The whole point of his ministry was a ministry that would not need his physical presence to continue. He built his replacement into the design from the beginning, and the church you sit in is the proof that it worked.

The leader who cannot do this has misunderstood the assignment. He thinks it was the work. It was always the workers.

So the question that ends this book is not whether you are doing good work. You may be. The question is whether anyone could do it after you — because you taught them, because you trusted them, because you were more committed to the kingdom continuing than to your own hands being on it. Not a following. Successors.

## The Towel, Passed

We began this book in an upper room, with a man who had all power kneeling on the floor with a basin and a cloth. That towel was the first image. Let it be the last.

A towel is meant to be passed. You do not wash one set of feet and frame the cloth. You wash, you wring it out, you hand it to the one who watched you, and you say what Jesus said:

> "For I have given you an example, that you should do as I have done to you." (John 13:15)

The whole inheritance of servant leadership is not a position to be held. It is a towel to be passed, from older hands to younger, generation reaching generation, until the Lord who first knelt comes back to finish what he started.

There will come a day when the work is no longer yours. It is coming for all of us. The only question that will matter then is whether you spent your strength making yourself necessary, or making yourself unnecessary — whether you held the towel, or handed it on.

Hand it on. Then let go. And if loosening your grip on the thing you love costs you more than you expected — good. The Servant who washed your feet did not cling to his own indispensability. He poured himself out, raised up his replacements, and trusted the Father with what came next.

Your turn to kneel, your turn to rise, your turn to put the towel in younger hands.
reflect: If you were removed from your ministry tomorrow, would it contract or continue — and what does your honest answer reveal about whether you have been building a body or building a following?
Name the faithful people you are currently teaching to teach others. If you cannot name them, what has been receiving the time and energy that should have gone to them?
Where are you still holding the towel out of love for the work, when love for the kingdom would mean handing it on — and what would it cost you to loosen your grip this year?
